# Questions & Hypotheses

1.	 How do adult birds with active nests change their provisioning behavior during hot periods? We hypothesized that adult birds will
a.	 (H1) reduce their provisioning rates during hot periods because they must put more time and/or energy into thermoregulation to avoid hyperthermia
b. (H1A) increase their provisioning rates during hot periods because they must deliver more energy to compensate for thermoregulatory costs to chicks (water or energy)

2. What mediates how responsive provisioning rates are to temperature?
a. (H1) Less optimal foraging conditions over the prior day will make provisioning rates less responsive to temperature because adults will respond to their chicks being hungrier when they were fed less over the prior day.
b. (H2) females in better condition (mass/tarsus) would be less likely than females in worse condition to reduce their visits during hot periods because they are able to mobilize the energy required to engage in more energetically costly active thermoregulatory behaviors and 
c.	(H3) Females with higher baseline cort will be less responsive to temperature - possibly because they are exposing themselves to suboptimal conditions
d. (H4) Females with higher stress-induced cort will be more responsive to temperature because they have been experiencing their environment as stressful, and therefore may not have extra energy to put towards thermoregulation during hot periods.

3.	How does heat affect female body condition and stress status? baseline and stress-induced?
a.	H1: Females that experienced worse heat over the prior week will be more likely to show reduced body condition.
b. H2: females that experienced heat over the prior day will be more likely to show elevated baseline corticosterone levels because they may upregulate their HPA axis in response to more challenging heat conditions
c.	H3: females that experienced heat over the prior week will be more likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels because challenging environmental conditions are correlated with elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels.

4.	 Does body condition mediate cort response?
a.	(H1) females in better body condition would be more likely to show elevated baseline cort after a hot period because they have the energetic capacity to respond to stress
b.	(H2) Females in better body condition would be less likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone after a hot period than females in worse body condition.

Q4 no longer really fits with this new organization.

# Go through count model eval process

1. Fit poisson regression, check for overdispersion & zero-inflation

```{r}
m <- glmer(valid_detections ~ poly(mean_temp_scaled,2) + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + site + (1 | site:attempt_id) + year_fct,
           family = "poisson",
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
					              !is.na(tod_h),
					              !is.na(site),
					              !is.na(attempt_id),
					              !is.na(year),
					              species == "WEBL"# ,
												# tod >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end <= hms::as.hms('17:00:00',tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
												) %>%
						mutate(across(c(tod_h,mean_temp,julian_date,mean_nestling_age),
													~ scale(.x)[,1],
													.names = "{.col}_scaled")), 
           )

check_overdispersion(m)
check_zeroinflation(m)
```

2. There is both overdispersion & zero-inflation, so we need to use negative binomial model

```{r}
m <- glmmTMB(valid_detections ~ poly(mean_temp_scaled,2) + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + site + (1 | site:attempt_id) + year_fct,
           family = nbinom2(),
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
					              !is.na(tod_h),
					              !is.na(site),
					              !is.na(attempt_id),
					              !is.na(year),
					              species == "WEBL"# ,
												# tod >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end <= hms::as.hms('17:00:00',tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
												) %>%
						mutate(across(c(tod_h,mean_temp,julian_date,mean_nestling_age),
													~ scale(.x)[,1],
													.names = "{.col}_scaled")), 
           )

check_overdispersion(m)
check_zeroinflation(m)
```

3. There is zero-inflation, so add zero-inflation factor to glmmTMB model

```{r}
m <- glmmTMB(valid_detections ~ poly(mean_temp_scaled,2) + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + site + (1|site:attempt_id) + year_fct,
           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ attempt_id,
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
```

Conclusion: use glmmTMB, negative binomial, with zero-inflation factor attempt_id (assuming that some pairs are just more likely to not feed than other pairs)

So provisining decreases with temp in forest, increases with temp in orchard, and does not change in grassland or row crop. Overall, no changes. So land cover is mediating responses to temp. So this means that the land cover interaction model is the one I should be using for provisioning. The causal links are interesting though - if condition mediates provioning responses to heat and land cover drives condtion, then adding land cover to the condition model might open a backdoor path and obscure the causal relationship between condition and provisioning.

Another question out of this is, are the adults responding to their own physiological state or are they responding to nestlings' condition? The tough part is that I could imagine that they're responding to nestlings' begging behavior. Does begging behavior peak at some intermediate condition (i.e. when nestlings are really hungry but not yet weakened by it), or is it strongest when nestlings are fed well?

From the reading, it looks like what we should expect is that in resource-poor environments (i.e. agriculture), provisioning should respond to quality of nestlings, whereas in resource-poor environments, provisioning should respond to need of nestlings. But also, in the short term, nestling begging rate is driven by hunger, and generally reduced in small nestlings in large broods.

So WEBL decrease provis with temp and TRES increase provis with temp.

## Q1H2

How do adult birds with active nests change their provisioning behavior during hot periods? We hypothesized that adult birds will

b.	(H2) I'd expect provisioning to be "peakier" during the present day (more focused on ideal temps) if the prior day had more ideal temps
provis ~ priordaytempgoodness + tnow^2

First step is to figure out how to quantify the "goodness" of the prior day. Just from the graphs of both species, detections peak at around 35C. So I'm going to take Danny's suggestion and measure prior day 5am-9pm degree hours difference from 35C. Higher means a "worse" temperature day, on one or both ends of the temp spectrum. I am slightly worried that the cooler temps will wash out the higher temps, or that we won't be able to tell whether the effect is from hot or cold temps, but scaling should help? I think I'll need to go back to the heat index calculation file to make those changes.

```{r}
p <- read_rds("../data/provis_manytempmeasures.rds")
```

## Q2H1

2.	How does female body condition mediates provisioning We hypothesized that females in better condition (mass/tarsus) would be 
a.	(H1) less likely than females in worse condition to reduce their visits during hot periods because they are able to mobilize the energy required to engage in more energetically costly active thermoregulatory behaviors


This implies an interaction between condition and temperature. I'm going to drop the habitat term from Q1H1

### WEBL

```{r}
           family = nbinom2(),
```


So for TRES, when females are in better body condition, there's more provisioning, and when it's hot, there's also more provisioning. But no interaction between the two.

## Q2H2

2.	How does female body condition mediates provisioning We hypothesized that females in better condition (mass/tarsus) would be 
a.	(H1) less likely than females in worse condition to reduce their visits during hot periods because they are able to mobilize the energy required to engage in more energetically costly active thermoregulatory behaviors and 
b.	(H2) more likely than females in worse condition to maintain total provisioning visits by increasing visit rates during cooler hours of the day.

## Q3H1

3.	How does heat affect baseline and stress-induced?
a.	H1: females that experienced heat over the prior day will be more likely to show elevated baseline corticosterone levels because they may upregulate their HPA axis in response to more challenging heat conditions
b.	H2: females that experienced heat over the prior week will be more likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels because challenging environmental conditions are correlated with elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels.

First step is to make sure that I have the right temp measures for cort

```{r}

c <- read_rds("../data/cort_manytempmeasures.rds")
```

Now on to the modeling. I'm going to keep replicating the model structure from q1. Now instead of provisioning being the response, cort is the response.

### WEBL

## Q4H1

4.	Are provisioning rates affected by circulating CORT levels? We hypothesized that 
a.	(H1) females with elevated baseline corticosterone concentrations after a hot period would be more likely to maintain provisioning delivery to nestlings during following hot periods because they have the capacity to upregulate their HPA axis in response to environmental challenges  (Mentesana and Hau 2022).




### WEBL

```{r}
m_WEBL <- glmmTMB(valid_detections ~ poly(mean_temp_scaled,2) * cort_s1_mother_scaled + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + brood_size_scaled + year_fct + (1|site:attempt_id),
           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ 1,
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
                                !is.na(cort_s1_mother),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
					              !is.na(brood_size),
					              !is.na(tod_h),
					              !is.na(site),
					              !is.na(attempt_id),
					              !is.na(year),
					              species == "WEBL"# ,
												# tod >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end <= hms::as.hms('17:00:00',tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
												) %>%
						mutate(across(c(tod_h,mean_temp,cort_s1_mother,julian_date,mean_nestling_age,brood_size),
													~ scale(.x)[,1],
													.names = "{.col}_scaled")), 
           )

m_WEBL_linint <- glmmTMB(valid_detections ~ mean_temp_scaled * cort_s1_mother_scaled + poly(mean_temp_scaled,degree = 2) + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + brood_size_scaled + year_fct + (1|site:attempt_id),
           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ 1,
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
                                !is.na(cort_s1_mother),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
					              !is.na(brood_size),
					              !is.na(tod_h),
					              !is.na(site),
					              !is.na(attempt_id),
					              !is.na(year),
					              species == "WEBL"# ,
												# tod >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end <= hms::as.hms('17:00:00',tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
												) %>%
						mutate(across(c(tod_h,mean_temp,cort_s1_mother,julian_date,mean_nestling_age,brood_size),
													~ scale(.x)[,1],
													.names = "{.col}_scaled")), 
           )

m_WEBL_noint <- glmmTMB(valid_detections ~ cort_s1_mother_scaled + poly(mean_temp_scaled,degree = 2) + poly(tod_h_scaled,2) + mean_nestling_age_scaled + brood_size_scaled + year_fct + (1|site:attempt_id),
           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ 1,
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),
                                !is.na(cort_s1_mother),
					              # !is.na(julian_date),
					              !is.na(mean_nestling_age),
					              !is.na(brood_size),
					              !is.na(tod_h),
					              !is.na(site),
					              !is.na(attempt_id),
					              !is.na(year),
					              species == "WEBL"# ,
												# tod >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end <= hms::as.hms('17:00:00',tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
												# tod_end >= hms::as.hms('11:00:00', tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
												) %>%
						mutate(across(c(tod_h,mean_temp,cort_s1_mother,julian_date,mean_nestling_age,brood_size),
													~ scale(.x)[,1],
													.names = "{.col}_scaled")), 
           )




c <- anova(m_WEBL,m_WEBL_linint,m_WEBL_noint) %>% tibble() %>% mutate(Model = c("No temp * LC interaction","Linear temp * LC interaction","Squared temp * LC interaction"),.before = Df)

(tab <- c %>%
  as.tibble() %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric),~round(.x,digits = 4)),
         P = `Pr(>Chisq)`) %>%
  dplyr::select(Model,AIC,Chisq,P) %>%
```

## Q4H2

4.	How does baseline and stress-induced cort mediate provisioning? We hypothesized that
a.	(H1) females with elevated baseline corticosterone concentrations would be more likely to maintain provisioning delivery to nestlings during hot periods because they have the capacity to upregulate their HPA axis in response to environmental challenges  (Mentesana and Hau 2022).
Look at this paper: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2656.12843
b.	(H2) Females with elevated stress-induced corticosterone concentrations would be less likely to maintain provisioning delivery to nestlings during hot periods because elevated stress-induced corticosterone may be a sign that females are experiencing their environment as challenging.

## Q4H3

c.	(H3) females with elevated baseline corticosterone concentrations would be more likely to maintain provisioning delivery to nestlings during hot periods after experiencing heat because they have the capacity to upregulate their HPA axis in response to environmental challenges  (Mentesana and Hau 2022). Prediction: negative cort * heat now2 * heat term, because expectation is less "peaky" than lower-cort females?
Look at this paper: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2656.12843
d.	(H4) Females with elevated stress-induced corticosterone concentrations would be less likely to maintain provisioning delivery to nestlings during hot periods after experiencing heat because elevated stress-induced corticosterone may be a sign that females are experiencing their environment as challenging. Prediction: positive cort * heat now2 * heat before term, because expectation is more "peaky" than lower-cort females

```{r}
                       breaks = c((20-mean_temp_tres_q4h3)/sd_temp_tres_q4h3,
                                  (25-mean_temp_tres_q4h3)/sd_temp_tres_q4h3,
                                  (30-mean_temp_tres_q4h3)/sd_temp_tres_q4h3,
                                  (35-mean_temp_tres_q4h3)/sd_temp_tres_q4h3,
                                  (40-mean_temp_tres_q4h3)/sd_temp_tres_q4h3),
                       # breaks = c(20,30,40,50),
                       # labels = c("20","30","40","50"),
                       # limits = c((15-mean(g$meanmaxtempI,na.rm = TRUE))/sd(g$meanmaxtempI,na.rm = TRUE),
                       #            (55-mean(g$meanmaxtempI,na.rm = TRUE))/sd(g$meanmaxtempI,na.rm = TRUE))
                       # limits = c(18,5)
    ) +
    # scale_linetype_manual(values = "solid") +
    ylim(0,300) +
    geom_text(data = dat_text_tres_q4h3, mapping = aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf,label = label),hjust = -.2, vjust = 1.2,inherit.aes = FALSE) # +
    #theme(legend.position = "none")
)

ggsave("../figures/provisbymaxtempxhab_TRES_q4h3.png",plot =  figq4h3_tres, width = 10, height = 6.6)
```


So, the salient interaction here is between mean temp and prior temp. When temps have been better prior, TRES are more responsive to temp. When it's been worse, they're less responsive to temp, and they provision less overall.

## Q4H4

d.	(H4) Females with elevated stress-induced corticosterone concentrations would be less likely to maintain provisioning delivery to nestlings during hot periods after experiencing heat because elevated stress-induced corticosterone may be a sign that females are experiencing their environment as challenging. Prediction: positive cort * heat now2 * heat before term, because expectation is more "peaky" than lower-cort females

```{r}
  rowwise() %>%

  dplyr::select(-c(count_ind, count_attempt)) %>%
```
